meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'No coward soul is mine, no trembler in the world's storm-troubled sphere'?
meta.ogDescription: Really Emily Brontë: the opening of her poem "No Coward Soul Is Mine" (written Jan 1846). Charlotte's "last lines" framing is the myth, not the words.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1818–1848 · English poet & novelist, author of Wuthering Heights
answer.sourceLine: These are the opening two lines of Emily Brontë’s poem “No Coward Soul Is Mine.” The wording is authentically hers — it matches her manuscript text (dated January 1846) word for word, including the punctuation. What is not reliable is the popular framing of it as her dying declaration: her sister Charlotte presented it posthumously as “the last lines my sister Emily ever wrote,” a claim scholars have since corrected.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Posthumously, c. 1850, in Charlotte Brontë’s selection of her sisters’ poems

source.excerpt:
No coward soul is mine,
No trembler in the world’s storm-troubled sphere:
I see Heaven’s glories shine,
And faith shines equal, arming me from fear.

O God within my breast,
Almighty, ever-present Deity!
Life — that in me has rest,
As I — undying Life — have power in thee!
trail: Emily’s autograph manuscript dates the poem to January 1846; it circulated only after her death, when Charlotte prefaced it “The following are the last lines my sister Emily ever wrote” (Wikisource).
That “last lines” framing is inaccurate: it is a late poem but “not, as her sister Charlotte imagined, her last” (Poetry Archive).
The opening couplet is stable across the manuscript and every standard edition, so the exact wording is not in dispute (LitCharts).
source.excerptNote: The quoted line is the poem’s opening couplet, shown here with the second stanza for context.
source.rightsNote: Emily Brontë died in 1848 and the poem entered print in the mid-19th century, so both the work and its text are long in the public domain in the United States (first published well before 1931).

author.name: Emily Brontë
author.heading: About Emily Brontë
author.bio: Emily Jane Brontë (1818–1848) was the middle of the three writing Brontë sisters and the author of the single novel Wuthering Heights (1847). She and her sisters first published under the male pen names Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell; Emily wrote as “Ellis Bell.” Fiercely private, she left a body of intense, metaphysical verse of which “No Coward Soul Is Mine” is the most celebrated. She died of tuberculosis in December 1848, aged 30.

misattribution.heading: The myths around a real quote
misattribution.intro: The words are genuinely Emily Brontë’s — the confusion is about when she wrote them and how they were introduced to the world.

items.why: Publishing the poem after Emily’s death, Charlotte prefaced it “The following are the last lines my sister Emily ever wrote” (Wikisource). But the manuscript is dated to January 1846, nearly three years before Emily died — it is a late poem, “not, as her sister Charlotte imagined, her last” (Poetry Archive).

items.who: Circulated as “No Coward Soul Am I”
items.why: The poem is sometimes cited under the altered title “No Coward Soul Am I” — the form linked to the American poet Emily Dickinson, who admired it and had it read at her funeral (annebronte.org). Brontë’s own opening line reads “No coward soul is mine.”

misattribution.truthLine: The line itself is authentic Emily Brontë; only the “dying words” story attached to it is unreliable (Poetry Archive).

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Written as Emily Brontë approached the end of her short life, “No Coward Soul Is Mine” is a defiant statement of inner faith — not the faith of church or creed, but a conviction that an “ever-present Deity” lives within the self and renders death powerless. It has become her most quoted poem.

Its afterlife is bound up with another great poet: Emily Dickinson kept the poem close, quoted it in letters, and it was reportedly read at her funeral in 1886 — one 19th-century recluse-poet’s tribute to another.
